description:
We have to connect the dots between different parameters and make sense out of them. That's why we'll be D-Detectives! Skills:

- Data analysis / ML

-  Graphic design

- Storytelling in front of judges
summary: We built an interactive website and short presentation that help people understand how Earth’s measurements change over time. Users choose a signal, such as global temperature or atmospheric carbon dioxide, and the tool shows what is changing, how much it changes per decade, where it changes most across latitude bands, and whether the change is statistically significant. Using NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 temperature data and NOAA’s Mauna Loa CO₂ record, we found that the Arctic has warmed more than three times as fast as the globe since 1980, while one Southern Ocean band shows no significant change in the same period. By turning complex data into clear answers, This will helps students, educators, and the public tell real trends from noise.
details:
The project has two parts. The website opens with a story in three parts (what is changing, where it is changing, and whether it is real), then gives users a working analysis lab. Users pick a dataset and a start year, and the lab answers four questions: what is changing, how much it changes per decade with a 95% range, where it changes most, and whether the change is statistically significant.

The lab uses two built-in official datasets: NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 zonal annual temperature means (global plus 14 latitude bands) and NOAA’s Mauna Loa annual carbon dioxide record. Users can also upload any NASA CSV table with a Year column. Each additional column is treated as a separate region or series, so the same analysis works on new variables.

For the statistics, we fit a least-squares trend to the yearly values. Yearly climate values are correlated from one year to the next, so we widen the uncertainty using the lag-1 autocorrelation of the residuals. This keeps us from overstating significance. Significance is tested at 95% confidence and reported as a p-value.

Key results: global temperature has risen about 0.21 °C per decade since 1980. The Arctic band (64°N to 90°N) has risen about 0.66 °C per decade, more than three times the global rate. The Southern Ocean band (44°S to 64°S) shows no significant change since 1980, which shows that a non-significant result is not the same as no change. Carbon dioxide rose from about 316 ppm in 1959 to 427.35 ppm in 2025, and the yearly increase grew from about 0.9 ppm per year in the 1960s to about 2.6 ppm per year in 2015 to 2025.

The impact we hope for is to let students, educators, journalists, and the public ask the questions scientists ask of Earth data, and see the difference between a real trend and noise. The site explains the statistics in plain language.

Tools: HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, with inline SVG charts and no external libraries, plus Google Fonts (Fraunces and Inter). The presentation is an HTML slide deck. The site is designed to be creative and accessible: a drifting starfield, a breathing Earth motif, a story-first structure, and support for reduced-motion settings.
